issue.issue_text: Whether the failure to put an incriminating circumstance to the accused during their examination under Section 313 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, by itself, vitiates the trial.

facts: During the examination of the accused appellants under Section 313 of the Code of Criminal Procedure (CrPC), the specific incriminating circumstance of "exhortation" was not put to them.
The gist of witness testimonies that delineated the exact roles played by the appellants was also not put to them during this examination.
The appellants raised this issue of non-compliance with Section 313 for the first time during their appeal.
The prosecution's case relied heavily on eyewitness testimony, and the appellants were questioned about this evidence.
law: The failure to put an incriminating circumstance to an accused during their Section 313 CrPC examination does not, by itself, automatically vitiate or invalidate the trial.
For a trial to be vitiated on this ground, the accused must demonstrate that the omission has caused them actual prejudice, resulting in a failure of justice.
The burden of proving that prejudice was caused rests on the accused.
If an appellate court finds that non-compliance has caused prejudice, it can order a retrial from the stage of the Section 313 examination.
application: The Court acknowledged the procedural error in not specifically questioning the appellants about the exhortation.
However, it applied the legal principle that this omission is not fatal to the conviction unless the appellants can prove they were prejudiced by it.
The Court found that the appellants had failed to demonstrate any such prejudice.
It noted that the core of the prosecution's case, which was the ocular evidence from eyewitnesses, was put to the appellants, and they had an opportunity to respond to it.
Since no prejudice was shown, the Court concluded that the conviction was not vitiated by the procedural lapse.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the argument, holding that the failure to put an incriminating circumstance to an accused under Section 313 CrPC does not, by itself, vitiate the trial. The trial is only invalidated if the accused can prove that this failure caused them actual prejudice, which was not demonstrated in this case.

issue.issue_text: Whether an omission in the examination under Section 313 Cr.P.C. is fatal to the prosecution case only if the accused can demonstrate that prejudice has been caused, resulting in a failure of justice.

facts: An incriminating circumstance, specifically the act of 'exhortation' (instigation), was not put to the appellants during their examination under Section 313 of the Criminal Procedure Code (Cr.P.C.).
The appellants challenged their conviction based on this omission for the first time before the Supreme Court.
law: The Court relied on established legal precedent, including the cases of *Shobhit Chamar v. State of Bihar* and *Alister Anthony Pareira v. State of Maharashtra*.

The established legal principle is that a failure to put an incriminating circumstance to an accused under Section 313 Cr.P.C. does not, by itself, automatically render the trial void or vitiate the conviction.
The burden is on the accused to establish that the omission has caused them actual prejudice, resulting in a failure of justice.
application: The Court applied a "prejudice test" to determine the effect of the omission.
It found that the appellants had not demonstrated any prejudice. They were aware of the accusation of exhortation because:
a) They were represented by counsel throughout the trial.
b) Their counsel had cross-examined witnesses specifically on the point of exhortation.
c) The First Information Report (FIR), which detailed their role as instigators, was put to them.

Since the appellants were fully aware of the incriminating evidence against them and had the opportunity to challenge it, the Court concluded that the failure to specifically question them on this point during the Section 313 examination did not cause any prejudice.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court held that an omission in the examination under Section 313 Cr.P.C. is fatal to the prosecution's case only if the accused can demonstrate that prejudice has been caused, leading to a failure of justice. As the appellants in this case failed to show any such prejudice, the omission did not vitiate their conviction.

issue.issue_text: Whether an appellate court should remit a matter for retrial to cure a defect in the Section 313 examination, especially after a long passage of time.

facts: The issue concerns a situation where a defect in the examination of an accused under Section 313 of the Criminal Procedure Code (CrPC) is identified at the appellate stage.
A significant amount of time has passed since the original trial.
The objection regarding the defective Section 313 examination was not raised at the trial court but for the first time on appeal.
law: An appellate court has several options when it finds non-compliance with Section 313 CrPC.
If the court believes the defect has caused prejudice to the accused, it *may* direct a retrial from the stage of the defective examination.
However, a challenge to a conviction based on a Section 313 defect cannot be entertained unless the accused demonstrates that prejudice has been caused.
If an objection to a defective Section 313 statement is not raised at the earliest stage (i.e., the trial court), it is assumed that no prejudice was felt by the accused.
An appellate court may decline to remit a matter for retrial specifically on account of the long time that has already been spent in the trial.
application: The Court reasoned that the timing of the objection is crucial. If the issue is raised for the first time on appeal, after the matter has been "allowed to linger on," the court is less inclined to order a retrial.
The Court balanced the need to cure a procedural defect against the practical consequences of ordering a retrial after a long delay.
It concluded that the passage of time is a valid reason for an appellate court to refuse to send the case back for a retrial.
Furthermore, the Court emphasized that without a clear demonstration of prejudice by the accused, the conviction can be sustained, and there is no need for a retrial to cure the defect.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court decided that an appellate court should reject remitting a matter for retrial to cure a defect in the Section 313 examination, especially after a long passage of time. The Court reasoned that such a delay makes retrial an inappropriate remedy, particularly when the objection was not raised at the trial stage and the accused has not demonstrated any resulting prejudice.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the failure to put an incriminating circumstance to the accused during their examination under Section 313 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, by itself, vitiates the trial.
appellant_arguments: The appellants challenged their conviction based on the non-compliance of Section 313 Cr.P.C., implying that the failure to put the specific incriminating circumstance of 'exhortation' to them was a procedural flaw that should invalidate the trial.
respondent_arguments: The failure to specifically put the circumstance of 'exhortation' to the accused did not vitiate the trial because they suffered no prejudice.

The appellants were fully aware of this incriminating circumstance as: (a) they were represented by counsel; (b) witness statements were recorded in their presence; (c) their counsel cross-examined witnesses on the point of exhortation; and (d) the FIR, which detailed their role as instigators, was put to them.
The plea of prejudice was raised for the first time before the Supreme Court and was not raised before the trial court or the High Court.

arguments.issue_text: Whether an omission in the examination under Section 313 Cr.P.C. is fatal to the prosecution case only if the accused can demonstrate that prejudice has been caused, resulting in a failure of justice.
appellant_arguments: The challenge to the conviction was based on the non-compliance of Section 313, suggesting that the omission itself is a fatal defect, irrespective of whether prejudice was demonstrated.
respondent_arguments: An omission in the Section 313 examination is not fatal unless the accused can show that they suffered prejudice.
The appellants in this case failed to demonstrate any prejudice caused to them by the omission.

arguments.issue_text: Whether an appellate court should remit a matter for retrial to cure a defect in the Section 313 examination, especially after a long passage of time.
appellant_arguments: The appellants implicitly argued for the trial to be vitiated, which could lead to a retrial to cure the procedural defect.
respondent_arguments: A retrial is unnecessary as the omission was not prejudicial and therefore did not constitute a fatal defect needing to be cured.
Raising such objections belatedly creates a difficult situation for both the prosecution and the accused, making a retrial impractical.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: An objection regarding a defect in a statement under Section 313 of the Code of Criminal Procedure must be raised at the earliest stage to allow the court to rectify the defect; if the objection is delayed, it may not be considered.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: A failure to put all incriminating circumstances to an accused during their examination under Section 313 Cr.P.C. will not, by itself, vitiate the trial. The omission is only fatal if the accused can demonstrate that it caused them prejudice. When the plea of non-compliance is raised for the first time at a late stage, such as before the Supreme Court, it can be assumed that no prejudice was actually felt by the accused.
legal_tests_applied: The Prejudice Test: An omission in the Section 313 examination does not ipso facto vitiate the trial unless it is shown that its non-compliance has prejudiced the accused.

The Timeliness of Objection Test: Where there is a delay in raising the plea of a defective Section 313 examination, or the plea is raised for the first time in the Supreme Court, it can be assumed that no prejudice had been felt by the accused.
why_appellant_lost: The challenge to the conviction based on non-compliance of Section 313 Cr.P.C. raised for the first time on appeal cannot be entertained unless the appellants demonstrate that prejudice has been caused to them.

The appellants failed to demonstrate any prejudice, as the court noted: "No such prejudice was demonstrated before us and, therefore, we are unable to accept the contention raised on behalf of the appellants."
Because the appellants raised the plea for the first time before the Supreme Court, the court could assume that no prejudice had been felt by them.
why_respondent_won: The court accepted the legal position that "where there has been a failure in putting those circumstances to the accused, the same would not ipso facto vitiate the trial unless it is shown that its non-compliance has prejudiced the accused."
The court found that the appellants had not met the burden of demonstrating prejudice, which is a prerequisite for a challenge based on non-compliance with Section 313 to succeed.
The court endorsed the principle that a delayed objection to a Section 313 examination weakens the claim of prejudice.
policy_considerations: Raising objections to a Section 313 statement at the earliest stage is in the interest of justice, as it allows the court to "make good the defect and record an additional statement."

Allowing such objections to be taken belatedly creates a "diﬃcult situation for the prosecution as well as the accused," making remedies like retrial impractical and undesirable after a long passage of time.
